title: How do global merchandise exports change over time?
gist: FRED Blog uses Dallas Fed data (1981-Aug 2026) to show global merchandise export growth is highly cyclical and synchronized, swinging from about -30% to +45% versus much smaller GDP moves. The dollar's strength distorts dollar-measured trade, and growth is currently picking up.

insights.claim: Global merchandise exports do not change smoothly; they ebb and flow with large changes in short spans.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Trade-linked assets face regime-like swings rather than gradual drift.
insights.quote: They ebb and flow and undergo large changes in relatively short spans.

insights.claim: Year-over-year export growth has generally ranged from about -30% to +45%, far wider than GDP swings.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Trade volumes carry much higher beta than output, which matters for cyclical exposure.
insights.quote: Export growth has generally ranged from about −30% to +45%

insights.claim: In the 2007-2009 Great Recession, US real GDP fell 4.3% while world trade shrank by as much as 34.6%, the largest drop in the dataset.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Trade fell roughly eight times as much as GDP in the worst episode.

insights.claim: Big-ticket purchases such as autos and machinery postponed by households and firms drive the outsized trade drops, and rebounds are correspondingly sharp.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Capital-goods and durables exporters are most exposed to both slumps and snapbacks.

insights.claim: Merchandise exports rise and fall together worldwide because exporters sell into the same global market, so demand shifts hit all at once.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Diversifying across exporting regions offers little protection in trade downturns.
insights.quote: Merchandise exports rise and fall together worldwide.

insights.claim: US exports followed the same path as other regions through the downturns of 2001, 2007-2009, and 2020.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The US is not insulated from global trade cycles.

insights.claim: The data measure exports in US dollars deflated by US consumer prices, so a stronger dollar lowers the dollar value of other countries' exports even if shipments are unchanged.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
entities: Dallas Fed Database of Global Economic Indicators
insights.so_what: Dollar-denominated trade data embed a currency effect that can exaggerate real trade weakness.

insights.claim: The 2015-16 global export slump is partly explained by an 11% one-year rise in the broad dollar index.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Dollar strength episodes coincide with measured trade recessions.

insights.claim: As of July 2026 global export growth is picking up, with uncertainty over whether it will average double digits as in the 1990s and 2000s or meager single digits as in the 2010s.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The growth regime (double vs single digit) is the key open question for trade-sensitive sectors.
insights.quote: It remains to be seen whether it will average double-digit growth
